subject: space
title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
question: Why is the Moon sometimes round and sometimes a thin smile?
steps: Half the Moon is always lit

steps.title: Sunlight lights the Moon
steps.text: The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight bounces off it. The Sun is very far away, so its light comes from one side, like light from a giant lamp.
steps.try: Drag the picture to look around. Find the Sun, the Earth and the Moon.
steps.see: The sides of the Earth and the Moon that face the Sun are bright. The sides facing away are dark.

steps.title: Half the Moon is always lit
steps.text: The Moon is a ball. Sunlight can only reach the half that faces the Sun. So one half of the Moon is always bright and the other half is always dark, wherever the Moon is.
steps.try: Watch the camera fly around the Moon. Drag the picture to stop it and look for yourself.
steps.see: From the Sun's side you see a full bright circle. From the far side you see almost no light. From in between you see a half or a thin slice.

steps.title: A trip around the Earth
steps.text: The Moon travels around the Earth. From one new moon to the next takes about 29 and a half days, which is about a month. The small window shows the Moon the way we see it from Earth.
steps.try: Move the slider to choose a day, or press Play.
steps.see: The lit half always faces the Sun. As the Moon moves, we see more or less of that lit half, so its shape seems to change.

steps.title: The names of the phases
steps.text: Each shape of the Moon is called a phase. Waxing means the bright part is growing. Waning means it is shrinking. In order they are: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter and waning crescent. Then it starts again.
steps.try: Slide the Moon to each dot on its path and read the name of the phase.
steps.see: At first quarter and last quarter we see half of the Moon's face lit. They are called quarters because the Moon is one quarter or three quarters of the way through its trip.

steps.title: It is not Earth's shadow
steps.text: Many people think the Earth's shadow makes the Moon change shape. It does not! Earth's shadow points away from the Sun. At first quarter and last quarter the Moon is nowhere near it. Even at full moon, the Moon's tilted path usually takes it just above or below the shadow. We made the tilt bigger here so you can see it.
steps.try: Turn on 'Line up for an eclipse' and watch what happens to the full moon.
steps.see: When the full moon moves right into Earth's shadow, it turns dark and reddish. That is a lunar eclipse. It can only happen at full moon, and it does not happen every month.

steps.title: Look up at the Moon
steps.text: Now you are standing on the Earth looking at the Moon. Watch it change over a whole month. The phases repeat again and again, about every 29 and a half days.
steps.try: Press Play and watch the Moon grow from a thin crescent to a full moon and shrink back again.
steps.see: In the northern half of the world the bright part grows from the right. In Australia and other southern places the picture is flipped, so it grows from the left.

quiz.q: What makes the Moon seem to change shape?
options: The Earth's shadow covers part of it
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it goes around the Earth
quiz.why: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see more or less of that lit half.

quiz.q: About how long is it from one full moon to the next?
quiz.why: The whole cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days, which is about one month.

quiz.q: Where is the Moon at new moon?
options: Between the Earth and the Sun
On the far side of the Earth from the Sun
quiz.why: At new moon the Moon's lit half faces the Sun, away from us, so we only see its dark side.
